transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, um, I guess... I guess they brought me in, like, my manager made me come. I work at this big distribution warehouse down by the interstate, moving freight and stuff. I used to take some classes at the community college, but now I just move boxes, mostly. But anyway, they made me come here because of what happens at work. 

It's really loud there, you know, lots of moving parts, but lately, I just... I keep doing these things. Like, I'll be standing right by the forklift—it's this big yellow stand-up reach truck—and I just freeze. Completely freeze. My arms will just go straight up in the air, right by the forklift, and I just hold them there, like I'm stuck. And then, well, the forklift makes this loud beeping sound when it reverses, and the spotters use these specific hand signals to guide it, and I just start copying them. I just start making the exact same beeping sounds out loud with my mouth, and doing the exact same hand signals they do. Over and over. 

And when I'm supposed to be stacking the freight, I don't do it the normal way on the pallets anymore. I have to move the boxes into these strange little patterns. Like, very specific little shapes and arrangements, sliding them around until they're exactly right, even if it doesn't match the manifest. And the whole time, the shift supervisor and the other guys are just yelling at me. They're screaming over the noise of the warehouse, telling me to stop, telling me I'm holding up the whole loading dock, but I don't stop. I just keep moving the boxes in my little patterns or standing there with my arms stuck up in the air making the noises. So, yeah, that's... they said I couldn't come back until I saw a doctor about it.

When you freeze with your arms up in the air or start making those beeping sounds and hand signals—do you feel like you're choosing to do these things, or do they just happen to you without you deciding to do them?

I don't... I mean, choosing is a really weird word for it. I don't really know how to explain it. You have to understand how it is on the floor first. The concrete is always vibrating from the machines, and the big yellow reach trucks have these specific backup alarms. It is this loud, piercing sound, and the pitch is exactly a B-flat, I think. I used to take a music theory class back at the community college before I started working full time, so I always notice things like the pitch of the machinery. 

But anyway, when I am standing there, it is not like I think to myself that I should put my arms up. But it is also not like someone else is pulling them up with invisible strings or something. It is just... they go up. And they stay there. And the air in the warehouse is always so drafty, especially right near the loading bay doors when the eighteen-wheelers back in, and I can feel the cold air on my wrists when my sleeves slide down from my arms being up so high. 

And the sounds, the beeping, it just comes out of my mouth. It feels like the sound is already in the air, just filling up the whole warehouse and bouncing off the corrugated metal roof, and my mouth just sort of joins in with the noise. The spotters wear these bright high-vis orange vests, and they do the hand wave, like a flat palm pushing back to guide the drivers, and my hand just does the flat palm too. 

So I do not really know if I am deciding to do it or not. The shift supervisor, Gary, he is always screaming over the noise asking why I am doing it, and I just look at him because I do not have a good answer. I am just in it. The boxes have to go in the pattern, the beep has to happen. It is not a choice like picking what to eat for lunch from the vending machine in the breakroom, it is just... what is happening on the dock at that exact second. I just don't know.

When did you first notice these things starting to happen—the freezing with your arms up, the beeping sounds, the hand signals? Did they all start around the same time, or did some of them begin at different points?

Well, um, it's hard to pinpoint exactly when it all started, you know? Because time gets a little blurry when you're working the same shift over and over. I work the second shift, so I get there right when the sun is starting to go down, and the light comes through those high clerestory windows in the warehouse in this really specific, dusty way. It catches all the cardboard dust in the air. 

But, if I really think about it, the freezing and the... the patterns with the boxes and the sounds... it hasn't just been a few days or anything. It's been going on for a while. I think it's been about six months now. Yeah, roughly six months of all this happening. 

I remember because it was right around the time they switched out the old wooden pallets for those new blue plastic ones, the ones that slip around if you don't stack the freight perfectly. And that's when I started needing to arrange the boxes in those specific shapes, because the blue pallets just didn't feel right. And then the freezing started happening, and the beeping... it all kind of rolled in together around that same time, about six months ago. Gary, the supervisor, he started getting really on my case about it back then, keeping a clipboard with all my times on it. So yeah, I'd say it's been half a year of this... this whole thing at the warehouse.

Before you freeze with your arms up or make the beeping sounds, do you feel any kind of tension, tingling, or uncomfortable sensation building up in your body or mind that gets relieved when you do these things? Or do unwanted thoughts or worries come into your head first that make you feel like you have to do them?

No, it's not like that. It's not a tension. Like, I know what you mean, like when you have an itch and you really have to scratch it, or when you're waiting for the microwave to beep and you're just staring at the numbers counting down, 3, 2, 1, and you feel that anticipation. It's not like that at all. There's no build-up. There's no worry. I'm not standing there thinking, "Oh, if I don't put my arms up, something terrible is going to happen to the warehouse," or "If I don't beep, the forklift is going to crash." My mind isn't doing that. 

Like I said, I guess they brought me in because at the warehouse I just keep doing these things. I'll just be standing there, and suddenly I'm freezing with my arms up by the forklift. Or the beeping starts, and I'm just copying the beeping sounds and the hand signals the spotters use. Or I'm moving the boxes in those strange little patterns on the blue plastic pallets, sliding them around until they fit the shape in my head, even when everyone is yelling for me to stop. Gary will be right there, his face getting all red under the fluorescent lights—they have those big high-bay LED fixtures now that make everything look kind of washed out and harsh—and he'll be screaming, "What are you doing? Stop! You're holding up the whole line!" But there's no feeling of relief when I do it. It's not like scratching an itch. It's just... the arms go up. The beep happens. The boxes go into the pattern. It's just what happens. It's just part of the warehouse now, like the dust in the air or the smell of the exhaust from the trucks.

If you really tried hard, or if your manager was standing right next to you watching, do you think you could stop yourself from putting your arms up, or making the beeping sounds, or arranging the boxes in those patterns? Or does it feel completely impossible to hold back, even for a few seconds?

Well, like I was just saying, he *is* standing right next to me. Gary, I mean. So it's not really a hypothetical situation where maybe I could stop if I tried really hard just because the boss is watching. He's right there. He wears these clear plastic safety glasses that always get fogged up around the edges because it gets so humid on the floor, especially when it's raining outside and the big bay doors are open, and he gets right up in my face. 

And like I told you, I guess that's exactly why they brought me in here to see you in the first place. Because I keep doing it anyway. I keep freezing with my arms way up in the air right by the 5,000-pound forklifts, and I keep copying the backup beeping sounds and doing the spotters' hand signals, and I keep moving the freight boxes around into those strange little patterns on the pallets. And I do all of that even when he is standing two feet away, literally yelling for me to stop. 

Everyone is yelling, honestly. The other guys on the line start yelling too because the main conveyor belt doesn't stop, you know? The motorized rollers just keep pushing more and more boxes down the line toward my station, and if I'm not loading them, they start piling up and getting crushed against the metal guardrails. And Gary is screaming, his face gets all red, and he's yelling, "Put your hands down! Load the pallet! What is wrong with you!" but... no, I can't stop it. 

It doesn't matter how hard I try or who is watching or how backed up the line gets. It's not like holding your breath where you can just force yourself to hold it in if you really concentrate. The arms just stay locked up. The sound just comes out of my throat to match the warehouse. The boxes just have to go into the pattern I see for them. I can't hold it back, not even for a single second, no matter how loud they yell at me to snap out of it. It just happens.

The detailed description of involuntary motor and vocal behaviors triggered by environmental stimuli (forklift sounds, hand signals, specific patterns), combined with inability to suppress them despite severe social/occupational consequences over 6 months, is highly consistent with Motor Tic Disorder (F95.1). The echolalia-like beeping and echokinesia-like hand signal copying further support tic disorder diagnosis.

opening_question.intent: Establish rapport and identify the chief complaint
opening_question.question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with multiple motor tics (arm freezing/dystonic posturing, echolalia/echokinesis with beeping sounds and hand signal imitation) and complex motor behaviors (box arrangement in specific patterns) that have persisted for approximately 6 months. The symptoms are involuntary, occur without premonitory tension or obsessive thoughts, and persist despite external pressure and consequences. The constellation of motor and vocal tics with functional impairment at work is most consistent with Persistent (Chronic) Motor or Vocal Tic Disorder (F95.1), specifically manifesting as a combined motor and vocal tic presentation.
